questions.statement: Choose the sentence that uses commas correctly around a non-defining relative clause.
questions.context: Semana W20 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 1 de 20 sobre non-defining relative clauses.

options.text: My sister, who lives in Ponce, is visiting us next week.
options.feedback: Correct! Both commas close around the extra information about the sister, which is not needed to identify her.

options.text: My sister who lives in Ponce is visiting us next week.
options.feedback: No. With no commas the clause becomes defining, and it would claim you have only one sister who lives in Ponce.

options.text: My sister, who lives in Ponce, is visiting us next week next week.
options.feedback: No. Repeating the time expression makes the sentence say the visit happens two times next week.

options.text: My sister who lives in Ponce, is visiting us next week.
options.feedback: No. A comma after the subject but not before the clause leaves the extra information badly marked.

questions.explanation:
Both commas close around the extra information about the sister, which is not needed to identify her. In this item the choice that works is 'My sister, who lives in Ponce, is visiting us next week.', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

questions.statement: Which relative pronoun is normally used after a preposition in a non-defining relative clause?
questions.context: Semana W20 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 2 de 20 sobre non-defining relative clauses.

options.text: whom
options.feedback: Correct! After a preposition, the object form 'whom' is used for people in a non-defining clause.

options.text: who
options.feedback: No. 'Who' is the subject form and cannot follow a preposition in this position.

options.text: which
options.feedback: No. 'Which' refers to things and never to a person, so it cannot fill this slot.

options.text: what
options.feedback: No. 'What' cannot function as a relative pronoun after a preposition.

questions.explanation:
After a preposition, the object form 'whom' is used for people in a non-defining clause. In this item the choice that works is 'whom', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

questions.context: Semana W20 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 3 de 20 sobre non-defining relative clauses.

options.text: which
options.feedback: Correct! The clause gives extra information about the car, and 'which' is the pronoun used for things in that role.

options.text: that
options.feedback: No. 'That' is not used in non-defining clauses, where the meaning would be ambiguous without the commas.

options.text: who
options.feedback: No. 'Who' refers to people, and a car is not a person.

options.text: whose
options.feedback: No. 'Whose' shows possession, but the sentence says nothing about who owns the car.

questions.explanation:
The clause gives extra information about the car, and 'which' is the pronoun used for things in that role. In this item the choice that works is 'which', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

questions.statement: Which sentence contains a NON-defining relative clause, rather than a defining one?

options.text: The concert, which was sold out in an hour, took place at the stadium.
options.feedback: Correct! Commas on both sides mark the clause as extra information about the concert, not the thing being named.

options.text: The concert that was sold out in an hour took place at the stadium.
options.feedback: No. Without commas the clause identifies which concert is meant, which makes it defining.

options.text: The concert, that was sold out in an hour, took place at the stadium.
options.feedback: No. 'That' cannot introduce a non-defining clause, so the commas are not enough to save it.

options.text: The concert which was sold out in an hour, took place at the stadium.
options.feedback: No. A single comma does not mark the clause as non-defining and leaves the sentence unbalanced.

questions.explanation:
Commas on both sides mark the clause as extra information about the concert, not the thing being named. In this item the choice that works is 'The concert, which was sold out in an hour, took place at the stadium.', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

questions.statement: What is the effect of removing the commas from: 'The results, which were surprising, changed the plan.'
questions.context: Semana W20 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 7 de 20 sobre non-defining relative clauses.

options.text: The clause becomes defining, so it would identify only the results that changed the plan.
options.feedback: Correct! Commas are what separate extra information from defining information, so taking them away changes the meaning.

options.text: The sentence becomes a question, because commas work like question marks.
options.feedback: No. Commas never create or remove interrogative structure; a question needs auxiliary inversion.

options.text: The clause becomes a passive voice construction with the auxiliary 'were'.
options.feedback: No. The passive voice is decided by the verb form 'were changed', not by punctuation.

options.text: The sentence keeps exactly the same meaning, since commas never change meaning in English.
options.feedback: No. Commas are meaning-bearing in English, which is exactly why the non-defining clause needs them.

questions.explanation:
Commas are what separate extra information from defining information, so taking them away changes the meaning. In this item the choice that works is 'The clause becomes defining, so it would identify only the results that changed the plan.', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

questions.statement: What kind of information does a non-defining relative clause usually add?
questions.context: Semana W20 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 14 de 20 sobre non-defining relative clauses.

options.text: Extra detail about something already identified, which the reader could do without.
options.feedback: Correct! Non-defining clauses add optional detail and always sit between two commas.

options.text: The essential detail needed to identify exactly which thing is meant.
options.feedback: No. Essential identifying detail is what defines a defining relative clause, which takes no commas.

options.text: A list of every other object that appears in the same sentence.
options.feedback: No. A relative clause carries one verb of its own; it does not list other objects.

options.text: A second main verb that must agree with the subject of the main clause.
options.feedback: No. Agreement of the main verb depends on the subject alone, not on any extra clause.

questions.explanation:
Non-defining clauses add optional detail and always sit between two commas. In this item the choice that works is 'Extra detail about something already identified, which the reader could do without.', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

questions.statement: Why can a non-defining relative clause never begin with the word 'that' in standard written English?
questions.context: Semana W20 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 19 de 20 sobre non-defining relative clauses.

options.text: Because 'that' introduces only defining clauses, which need no surrounding commas.
options.feedback: Correct! Restrictive clauses use 'that', and it is precisely those defining clauses that take no commas.

options.text: Because 'that' is a preposition and cannot follow the comma in this position.
options.feedback: No. 'That' is a determiner and a conjunction here, never a preposition before a clause.

options.text: Because a clause starting with 'that' must always be a question in inverted order.
options.feedback: No. A 'that' clause is not a question and shows no auxiliary inversion.

options.text: Because 'that' can only refer to objects and never to the subject of the sentence.
options.feedback: No. 'That' refers to people or things equally in defining clauses; it is not limited to objects.

questions.explanation:
Restrictive clauses use 'that', and it is precisely those defining clauses that take no commas. In this item the choice that works is 'Because 'that' introduces only defining clauses, which need no surrounding commas.', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.
